title: Finish your first draft: a word-goal plan that actually holds
summary: How to pick a daily goal you'll keep, what to do on bad days, and how to stop rewriting chapter one forever.

body.p: The hardest part of a first book isn't talent. It's getting to the end. A small goal you hit most days beats a big goal you quit.

body.h: Pick a goal you could hit on a bad day

body.p: If 1,000 words a day sounds good, set 300. You'll often go past it, and on hard days you'll still win. Set it as your daily goal in the Author Studio and watch your streak grow.

A 60,000-word novel at 300 words a day is about 200 writing days. At five days a week, that's under ten months. A 25,000-word nonfiction book is about four months. Seeing the finish line makes it real.

Write forward. If you notice something to change in an earlier chapter, put a note in your book's notes and keep going. Editing comes after the draft exists. Most unfinished books have a perfect chapter one.

list: Don't try to make it up. Just hit today's goal.
Write for 10 minutes instead of a word count.
Re-read your last paragraph and write the very next sentence. That's usually enough to get going.

body.p: Upload your manuscript to your book's Manuscript folder at the end of each week. Every upload is kept as its own version, so you can always go back if a big change doesn't work out.

body.tip: Tell one person your goal and your finish date. Being accountable to someone doubles the odds you keep going.
